language.howToChooseYourGradeIntro: Our curriculum Grades K to 6 corresponds with ages:
language.howToChooseYourGradeContent:
It’s very important children start at the right level, have fun in learning and work at their own pace. Please help the children selecting the level that is not too easy, but also not too difficult for them. There are two ways to do this.

  • You can either check the learning goals yourself to determine the correct level for your child(ren).
  • Or you can let the child take several lessons to determine his or her level. For example, if your child has the age of 6, please let him or her take one lesson in grade K, one lesson in grade 1, and one lesson in grade 2 to determine at which level he or she is.

dialog.text: Hello, I am Tim.
Hello friends! My name is Ian. My father sails a boat that takes people on cruises through Loch Ness. I like to travel with him when I don't have school!

Today during this cruise, I am reading the new science book I got for my birthday. I am learning so much about the three states of matter: solid, liquid, and gas. For example, I learned that when liquid loses heat, it freezes and becomes solid.

When a solid gains enough heat, it will melt and change to liquid. When a liquid is heated to its boiling point, it evaporates and becomes a gas! This is how solid water (ice) changes to liquid water, and eventually becomes a gas, called steam.
I am going to keep a science journal about all the things I learn! Can you help me fill my journal?
Come on let's help Ian. I am sure this is going to be fun!

I learned in my science book that there are different scales used to measure temperature such as Celsius and Fahrenheit. While most countries measure temperature using the Celsius scale, people in the United States usually use Fahrenheit.

Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius (0°C), or 32 degrees Fahrenheit (32°F). This is called the freezing point of water. Below the freezing point, water is solid, and above the freezing point, water is liquid.
Can you help me organize these pictures in my science journal?

I learned in my book that all matter expands and contracts when it changes states. Most materials, such as metal, oil, and rocks, expand when they are heated. These materials expand as they change their state from solid to liquid (melt) and from liquid to gas (evaporate). They contract, or shrink, as they cool down.

But guess what? Water does not follow this rule. Water expands when it freezes. This means that ice takes up more space than liquid water. When ice gains heat, it contracts as it melts to liquid water, and then it expands again when it evaporates.
I want to add this new information to my journal. Can you help me sort these materials?
